widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def fit_poly_mse(x, y, x_test, y_test, degree):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    x_test = np.asarray(x_test, float)
    y_test = np.asarray(y_test, float)
    lo, hi = x.min(), x.max()
    z = 2 * (x - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    z_test = 2 * (x_test - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    coef = np.polyfit(z, y, degree)
    train = np.mean((np.polyval(coef, z) - y) ** 2)
    test = np.mean((np.polyval(coef, z_test) - y_test) ** 2)
    return round(float(train), 4), round(float(test), 4)

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_spreads(n, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = rng.uniform(0, 8.5, n).round(2)
    f = (4 + 2.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 8.5)
         + 0.8 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * t / 8.5))
    y = (f + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)).round(2)
    return t, y

hints.text: Rescale the test hours with the training `lo` and `hi`, not their own.
`coef = np.polyfit(z, y, degree)`, then `np.polyval(coef, z)` predicts.
Train MSE is the mean of `(np.polyval(coef, z) - y) ** 2`; test MSE does the same with `z_test` and `y_test`.

feedback.correct: At degree 3 on the lesson's data: (0.4045, 0.4614), as on the chart.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fit on the training rows only, and rescale both sets with the training `lo` and `hi`.

explain.text: Rescaling changes no fitted value, only the arithmetic: any polynomial in $t$ is a polynomial in $z$ of the same degree. Using the training `lo` and `hi` for the test rows keeps the test set out of the fit.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_spreads(n, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = rng.uniform(0, 8.5, n).round(2)
    f = (4 + 2.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 8.5)
         + 0.8 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * t / 8.5))
    y = (f + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)).round(2)
    return t, y

def fit_poly_mse(x, y, x_test, y_test, degree):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    x_test = np.asarray(x_test, float)
    y_test = np.asarray(y_test, float)
    lo, hi = x.min(), x.max()
    z = 2 * (x - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    z_test = 2 * (x_test - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    coef = np.polyfit(z, y, degree)
    train = np.mean((np.polyval(coef, z) - y) ** 2)
    test = np.mean((np.polyval(coef, z_test) - y_test) ** 2)
    return round(float(train), 4), round(float(test), 4)

screens.title: A perfect fit
screens.prose: An analyst models the spread with powers of the hour, then adds day-of-week and month dummies. Each addition lowers the in-sample error. With 30 terms on 30 rows the in-sample error is zero. They call it the best spread model on the desk.
screens.question: What is the right response?

options.text: Keep adding terms while the in-sample error falls
options.why: You chose by training error. It falls with every term, signal or noise, so it cannot say when to stop.

options.text: Accept it: zero error cannot be beaten
options.why: Zero error on the fitted rows is guaranteed with 30 terms on 30 rows. It says nothing about new days.

options.text: Score each candidate on held-out days and keep the one with the lowest test error
Check that $R^2$ is close to 1, then use it
options.why: $R^2$ in sample is 1 minus the training error over the variance. It is 1 here by construction.

hints.text: What happens to in-sample error when you add a term, any term?
With as many terms as rows, the fit interpolates: zero error, whatever the data.
Only rows the fit never saw can tell a real pattern from memorised noise.

feedback.correct: Only held-out error can rank the candidates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In-sample error falls with every added term.

byKey.keep: You chose by training error. It falls with every term, so it cannot say when to stop.
byKey.best: Zero in-sample error is guaranteed with 30 terms on 30 rows. It says nothing about new days.

explain.text: On the spreads, degree 15 already scores 0.091 in sample and 80.15 out of sample. A perfect in-sample fit is the symptom of overfitting, not the cure. Choose the model on rows it never saw.

screens.title: Why training error never rises
screens.prose: We saw it on every screen. Now prove it. Compare least squares fits of degree $d$ and $d + 1$ on the same training rows. Put the lines in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: The degree-$d$ fit is also a degree-$(d+1)$ polynomial, with top coefficient 0
So the degree-$(d+1)$ search includes the degree-$d$ fit among its candidates
Least squares returns the candidate with the smallest training MSE
So training MSE at degree $d + 1$ is at most that at degree $d$
The test rows took no part in the search, so the test MSE is free to rise

hints.text: Start with a fact about the smaller model.
A polynomial of degree $d$ is a special case of degree $d + 1$.
The smaller model sits inside the bigger set, and least squares picks the best of the set. So the bigger set does at least as well. The test rows come last.

feedback.correct: A bigger search can only match or beat a smaller one on the rows it searches.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the smaller model being a special case of the bigger one.

explain.text: Nested models: every degree-$d$ curve is available at degree $d + 1$. So training error is a non-increasing function of flexibility, by construction. That is why it cannot choose the degree.

screens.title: Forty knobs, ten years
screens.prose: A trend strategy has 40 parameters: look-backs, thresholds and stops. A researcher tunes all 40 on daily data for 2014 to 2023. On that period the Sharpe ratio is 2.6. The strategy has never traded a day outside it.
screens.question: What is the best estimate of its live Sharpe ratio?

options.text: About 2.6, since ten years is a long sample
options.why: Ten years is the period the 40 parameters were tuned on. Like training MSE, its Sharpe flatters the fit.

options.text: Unknown until it is scored on data the tuning never touched; expect it to be lower
Higher, because markets will repeat the same regimes
options.why: Tuning fits the regimes of 2014 to 2023, noise included. The next decade has its own.

options.text: Exactly zero, because every backtest is overfitted
options.why: Overfitting biases the in-sample number upwards. It does not prove the strategy has no edge.

hints.text: Which data chose the 40 parameters?
The Sharpe ratio of 2.6 is measured on the same days used to tune the parameters.
That is a training score. An honest estimate needs a held-out period, and it is usually lower.

feedback.correct: The 2.6 is an in-sample score; only held-out days can estimate the live one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which days set the parameters and which days measured the Sharpe ratio.

byKey.same: Ten years is the period the 40 parameters were tuned on. Its Sharpe flatters the fit, like training MSE.

explain.text: A backtest tuned and scored on the same decade is training error in disguise. Forty knobs can memorise that decade's regimes, its crashes and rallies included. Hold out a later period, or use the `validation` course's time-ordered folds, before trusting any number.

ideas: Training error never rises as a model gets more flexible: a bigger model can always copy a smaller one.
Test error is U-shaped in flexibility. Left of the bottom the model **underfits**; right of it, it **overfits**, fitting noise.
More training data narrows the gap between training and test error, but the test error never falls below the noise.

formula.name: Choosing by test error
formula.note: The fit $\hat f_d$ uses only the training rows. Degree 0 is the mean; degree $n - 1$ interpolates.

summary.trap: Choosing the degree, or adding features, by in-sample error always ends at the most flexible model: zero training error, worst test error.

quiz.prose: Thirty training spreads have mean 3.654 bp and variance 3.516 bp², dividing by $n$. You fit a polynomial of degree 0.
quiz.question: What training MSE does the degree-0 fit get?

widget.accept: 3.516: the fit is the mean, so its MSE is the variance.
widget.label: Training MSE

feedback.correct: The flat line sits at the mean, and its MSE is the variance, 3.516.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A degree-0 polynomial is a constant. Which constant minimises squared error?

byKey.sd: That is the standard deviation. The MSE of the mean is the variance itself.
byKey.mean: 3.654 is the fitted value, not its error.
byKey.zero: A flat line cannot pass through 30 scattered dots.

explain.text: A degree-0 polynomial is a constant, and least squares puts it at the mean. Its MSE is $\frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2$, the variance: 3.516.

options.text: B
D
options.why: D has the lowest training error, which is the number that lies. Its test error is the worst.

options.text: A
options.why: A has the smallest gap between the errors, but a small gap is not the goal. B's test error is lower.

options.text: C
options.why: C fits the training rows better than B, yet does worse on new rows: it has started to overfit.

feedback.correct: B has the lowest test MSE.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank the models by test MSE alone.

explain.text: Rank by test MSE: B at 0.52 beats C at 0.61, A at 0.85 and D at 3.10. D's tiny training error is the sign of overfitting.

quiz.prose: A regime model is trained on 2019 to 2021 and its training accuracy is 99%. On 2022 it is right 51% of the days, about as often as a coin.
quiz.question: Which explanation fits best?

options.text: It memorised the training period's regimes, noise included, and learned little that carries over
2022 data must be wrong, since the model was 99% accurate
options.why: You trusted the training score over the test score. The test score is the honest one.

options.text: It needs more parameters to capture 2022
options.why: More parameters raise training accuracy further and usually make the overfit worse.

options.text: The 99% was bad luck on the training set
options.why: Luck would not push training accuracy up to 99%. Flexibility does.

feedback.correct: A big gap between training and test performance is the mark of overfitting.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the training and test numbers.

explain.text: 99% in sample and 51% out of sample is the U at its right edge. The model memorised 2019 to 2021. Only the 2022 number estimates how it will trade.

quiz.prose: A degree-12 polynomial has test MSE 2.4 when trained on 30 days. The noise variance is 0.36.
quiz.question: Trained on 3,000 days from the same process, its test MSE will most likely be:

options.text: close to 0.36, a little above it
about 2.4 again
options.why: The coefficients are pinned down far better by 3,000 rows. The overfitting shrinks with data.

options.text: well below 0.36
options.why: No model beats the noise on average. 0.36 is the floor.

options.text: higher than 2.4
options.why: More rows make a flexible fit steadier, not wilder.

feedback.correct: More data pins the coefficients down, so the test error falls towards the noise floor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what 3,000 rows do to 13 coefficients.

explain.text: With 3,000 rows the 13 coefficients cannot chase individual dots, so the overfit fades. The test MSE approaches the noise variance, 0.36, from above, as degree 15 did with 300 days.
